title: A summary of benchmarking constrained, multi-objective and surrogate-assisted optimization methods
contribution: Formally extends convergence plots and accuracy, performance and data profiles to constrained problems with infeasible starts, multi-objective problems (hypervolume-based accuracy) and surrogate-assisted methods (effective evaluation count N = Nt + w*Ns), with RunnerPost as the open-source implementation (text read = GERAD G-2025-36 preprint).
problem_entry: Classical benchmarking tools implicitly assume feasible points are free, a single objective and no surrogates (p. 10); effort is measured in simulation calls (p. 4).
key_idea: Keep the four classical tools and change only their inputs: two-phase h-then-f convergence plots and a common f0 over first feasible values (pp. 10-11); normalized hypervolume s_acc (pp. 12-13); effective count N = Nt + w*Ns or CPU time (pp. 14-15).
assumptions: f: X -> R U {inf}, quantitative constraints c <= 0, hidden-constraint failures logged as inf/NaN, comparable stopping criteria across algorithms (pp. 4-5); h definition as extracted uses Omega where X seems meant (p. 10).
proof_devices: -log10(1-f_acc) >= d <=> f_acc >= 1-10^-d turns accuracy into correct decimals (p. 7)
explicit handling of degenerate instances: drop and flag when no algorithm improves f0 (p. 6)
experiments: None on real solvers; anonymized designed data plotted with RunnerPost to show time-vs-evaluation reversal, tau-dependent reversal, switching phenomenon, f0-choice robustness and w = 0 vs 1/10 (pp. 4, 6, 10-16).
positioning: Extends Dolan-More, More-Wild, Beiranvand-Hare-Lucet and Gould-Scott without criticism; borrows h from filter methods and the constraint taxonomy of Le Digabel-Wild (pp. 7-10, 12).
writing: Uniform template per tool (definition, example figure, axis conventions, worked reading) and prescriptive should-rules with little hedging (pp. 6-8).
limits_future: Methodology + software; combination of extensions asserted not shown (p. 16), hypervolume hard beyond two objectives (p. 13), w left to the user (p. 15); no concrete future work.

method_links.note: Is the benchmarking summary cited in Method 5; formalizes evaluation currency, several tau, whole-set profiles; the SKILL.md limitation about not having read it in full can be lifted.
Bounds step 3: do not compare DFO with derivative-based algorithms and keep the number of algorithms very low because of switching.
Hidden-constraint failures logged as inf/NaN; h over quantifiable constraints only; two-phase plots for infeasible starts.
RunnerPost as the group's shared benchmarking instrument, reused by S156 and S157.

transferable: Draw profiles of surrogate-assisted methods against N = Nt + w*Ns for at least two weights at equal budget (p. 15).
For infeasible starts, plot h up to the first feasible point and then the best feasible f (pp. 10-11).
Define f0 identically for all algorithms (min or max of first feasible values) and check the conclusion under the other choice (p. 11).
Remove the best solver and replot performance profiles to detect the switching phenomenon (p. 9, pp. 13-14).
Drop and flag instances where no solver improves f0 instead of dividing by zero (p. 6).
Log evaluation number, f (inf/NaN on failure) and a feasibility flag for every evaluation (p. 5).

quotes.text: Of course, having a large test set is preferable to a smaller one, but having a test set that is representative of the ultimate goal is crucial.
Moreover, comparing DFO algorithms to algorithms that explicitly use derivatives should be avoided.

title: A partitioned optimization framework for structure-aware problems
contribution: Introduces the partitioned optimization framework (reformulate min phi over Y as min Phi(x) = phi(gamma(x)) over a low-dimensional partition index) and proves that DFO with a covering step on the reformulation yields (generalized) local solutions of the original, possibly infinite-dimensional and discontinuous, problem.
problem_entry: Problems where fixing a few combinations of variables makes the rest easy, motivated by optimal control with discontinuous Mayer cost (parachute landing on rings) and composite greybox problems (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Partition Y into Y(x), let an oracle gamma(x) solve each restricted problem, and run a covering-step DFO method on Phi(x) = phi(gamma(x)) so the solver sees dim(X) <= 10 instead of dim(Y) ~ 100 or infinity (pp. 5-8, 19-20).
assumptions: Continuous index map chi and piecewise uniformly continuous gamma on a locally finite partition (Assumption 1, p. 6), plus boundedness/ample continuity sets (Assumption 2, p. 7); exact global oracle and infinite runs admitted unrealistic (p. 7, p. 26).
proof_devices: generalized local solution: neighborhood infimum of the barrier function equals the least accumulation value (Def. 1, p. 6)
pointwise bound phi(y) >= Phi(chi(y)) for all feasible y (p. 10)
neighborhood pull-back via continuity of chi (Lemma 3, p. 9)
finite accumulation set ACC(gamma;x) from locally finite partition + uniform continuity + completeness (Lemma 4, p. 9)
inf ACC(Phi;x) >= min over ACC(gamma;x) of inf ACC(phi_Omega;y) (Lemma 6, p. 10)
Theorem 2 = covering-step convergence (Prop. 1 from [3]) + assumption transfer (Prop. 2) + Theorem 1 (p. 11)
experiments: Four 2-3 variable problems from 8 starting points with first-iteration-to-tolerance tables (pp. 14-19); 100-variable variants vs NOMAD and PRIMA/BOBYQA from 6 random starts with cost model 1 unit per phi and 1+tau per Phi (pp. 19-25); failures and local-minimizer convergence reported (pp. 17, 22, 23).
positioning: Between parametric and bilevel optimization; complementary to high-dimensional DFO (active subspaces, random directions) and composite greybox methods; competitors explicitly not discredited (p. 4, p. 20).
writing: Illustrative 2D example solved in the introduction, fourfold contribution with section roadmap, a Remark after each assumption arguing it is mild in practice, one-sentence purpose before each lemma, self-audit of tightness (pp. 2-10, 26).
limits_future: Oracle gamma is the stringent requirement, no generic check of assumptions, covering step absent from popular solvers, useful only if N_ref*tau < N_ini (pp. 26-27); future: approximate local oracles, progressive barrier on the reformulation, learned partitions, counterfactuals (pp. 27-28).

method_links.note: Guarantee ladder global/local/generalized local and explicit audit of which hypotheses each rung uses; no necessity counterexamples, only examples where the sufficient condition fails but the conclusion holds.
The proof-carrying component is a covering step placed before any core algorithm rather than a Poll; Search skipped in experiments; covering step said likely optional in practice.
Grey-box structure (explicit f and phi-tilde, blackbox sigma and epsilon) exploited with a direct-search outer loop.
Extreme barrier on the reformulation; plan to switch to a progressive barrier with an infeasibility measure inherited from the subproblems.
Best-value-vs-cost curves on constructed problems rather than profiles, but the inner solve is charged (1+tau) and the claim is narrowed to POf-suited problems.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Min over a partition index of the value of an inner solver restricted to that partition set, with optimality transferred back by Theorem 1.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Common evaluation currency with explicit cost weights
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Each reformulated evaluation costs 1+tau units; largest winning tau reported; break-even rule N_ref*tau < N_ini.
Algorithm 1 accepts any iterative algorithm A; Theorem 1 accepts any solution of the reformulation (shared with S157).

transferable: Reformulate over the few variable combinations that make the problem easy: Phi(x) = phi(gamma(x)) with gamma an inner solver (pp. 5-6, 13-14).
Transfer optimality from a reformulation with the bound phi(y) >= Phi(chi(y)) and a neighborhood pull-back via continuity of chi (p. 10).
State results for generalized local solutions when the objective is discontinuous and the feasible set is not closed (p. 6).
Charge the inner solve as 1+tau units per outer evaluation and report the largest tau at which the method still wins, plus a break-even rule (pp. 19, 25, 27).
Report local convergence as the first iteration within +-5E-3, +-5E-6, +-5E-9 of x* over several starts (pp. 14-19).
When a naive implementation fails, name the missing ingredient and show a stronger solver on the same reformulation does better (pp. 23, 25).
Solve the running example informally in the introduction before the formal framework (p. 2).

quotes.text: What makes the DFPOm efficient is the sheer dimension reduction provided by the POf.
Yet, the proof of Theorem 1 actually shows that our analysis is not tight.

title: Benchmarking Bilevel Derivative-Free Optimization Algorithms
contribution: Proposes a bilevel DFO benchmarking methodology: an a-posteriori refereeing procedure (End-Point, Complete, Reverse) that revokes non-admissible points, a scaled effort N = lambda*N_UL + N_LL with (nx+1)(ny+1) data-profile groups, and the open-source BOLIB.jl test set.
problem_entry: Existing bilevel DFO benchmarks do not validate lower-level optimality and miscount effort, so an inefficient lower-level solver can look best with falsely admissible points (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Re-solve the lower level at claimed-admissible points with a referee and revoke those it beats by more than eps_obj, then profile the filtered logs against a cost-weighted effort (pp. 11-14).
assumptions: Optimistic bilevel form; inexact eps-feasibility/rationality/admissibility (Defs. 1-2, p. 5); constraints scaled to one tolerance; referees refute but never certify and use identical settings across algorithms (pp. 11-13).
proof_devices: cost analysis of referee strategies: End-Point proportional to |P|, Complete to history length, Reverse in between (p. 12)
deterministic Complete and Reverse referees find the same final admissible point (claim without proof, p. 12)
(nx+1)(ny+1) grouping reduces to np+1 when ny = 0 and equals one failed bilevel poll with minimal positive bases (p. 14)
experiments: 67 BOLIB instances in Julia, N_UL = 300, N_LL = 100*ny, eps = (1e-9, 0), tau in {1e-1,1e-2,1e-4}, anonymized Algo1-3; effort-currency test with lambda = 60; external referee test; internal referee test with CS / MADS / MADS+quad from NOMAD recovering the expected hierarchy; refereeing CPU times reported (pp. 15-19).
positioning: Tabulated review of 20 bilevel DFO methods by upper-level scheme, lower-level exactness and benchmarking type (Table 1, p. 10); specific critiques of undefined accuracy values, upper-level-only counting (including coauthor Diouane's prior work) and nx*ny+1 grouping (pp. 8-9, 14).
writing: Four contribution bullets, a short failure story as motivation, an In-summary paragraph after each test; conclusion recommends Reverse although Section 4.4 found End-Point best in its example (pp. 3-4, 17, 19).
limits_future: Referee cost can exceed the optimization cost, End-Point is myopic, referee start at y_k may revoke almost everything, only analytic problems (pp. 11-15, 19); no future-work section.

method_links.note: Evaluation currency made explicit for two levels, data profiles at several tau with dimension-normalized groups, benchmarking CPU cost reported.
Competitors anonymized as Algo1-3 rather than named with settings, as in S128's anonymized data.
Counterexample logic moved from theorems to benchmark logs: revocation needs an explicit witness y_r and the referee never certifies.
BOLIB ported to the open-source Julia package BOLIB.jl.
NOMAD's CS, MADS and MADS with quadratic search used as a controlled ladder of lower-level solvers.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A posteriori re-optimization revokes claimed solutions only with an explicit better lower-level point; never certifies admissibility.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Without refereeing CS/MADS/MADS+quad ranking is scrambled; with any referee the expected order is recovered.

Use a Reverse referee (walk the history backward to the first non-revoked point) to match Complete-referee conclusions at about half the cost (pp. 12, 17).
Validate a new benchmarking protocol on a nested algorithm family with a known ranking (p. 17-19).

The Reverse Referee is our recommended approach, as it leads to conclusions similar to those of the Complete Referee while requiring a least computational cost.

title: Surrogate-based categorical neighborhoods for mixed-variable blackbox optimization
contribution: Builds categorical neighborhoods from GP surrogates of the objective and constraints (kernel-induced distance, feasibility-first constraint pseudo-distance, dominance-based ordering) and plugs them into CatMADS as CatMADSGP, which outperforms CatMADS, Pymoo and Optuna on Cat-Suite data profiles.
problem_entry: Neighborhood-based mixed-variable methods use user-defined (MV-MADS) or objective-only (CatMADS) neighborhoods that ignore constraint behavior across categories; BO lacks local guarantees (pp. 4-6).
key_idea: Rank candidate categories by a kernel distance d_f and a constraint pseudo-distance d_g that is zero when both are predicted feasible, using Pareto dominance with the primary criterion switching on incumbent feasibility, and use the m first as the categorical poll neighborhood (pp. 12-16).
assumptions: Relaxable-quantifiable constraints define Omega, unrelaxable and hidden constraints give f = +inf, finite categories, no meta variables, noiseless GPs; theory inherited from the CatMADS framework (pp. 3, 10, 21).
proof_devices: kernel-induced metric d(u,v) = k(u,u)+k(v,v)-2k(u,v) = ||phi(u)-phi(v)||^2 via Moore-Aronszajn (eq. 11, p. 12)
pseudo-distances that keep symmetry and triangle inequality but drop identity of indiscernibles by design (pp. 12-14)
framework-membership argument: the method remains an instance of CatMADS, so convergence results are unchanged (p. 21)
experiments: Mechanical-part case study (surrogate neighbors find 4 feasible of 6 vs 0 for Gower and objective-based, pp. 16-17); 200-evaluation runs from a common infeasible 40-point DoE over several seeds (pp. 22-23); Cat-Suite 60 problems x 3 seeds, budget 250n, data profiles at tau in {1e-2,1e-3,1e-5} vs CatMADS, Pymoo GA, Optuna (pp. 23-25); no BO baseline and no ablation of the added BO search step.
positioning: Defined against CatMADS (objective-only IDW neighborhoods) and MV-MADS (user-defined neighborhoods); metaheuristic operators viewed as neighborhoods; kernels borrowed from BO (p. 6, pp. 9-10).
writing: One-sentence research gap and four numbered objectives, a toy supplier/material/shape problem threaded through the paper, a Hamming mini-example; scope explicitly limited to structural information rather than a new optimizer (pp. 5, 7, 12).
limits_future: GP construction cost and capped BO step acknowledged (pp. 12, 22); future: adaptive number of neighbors and meta variables (p. 26); missing BO baseline, missing ablation and a 24-vs-32 component inconsistency not addressed (pp. 7, 16, 22).

method_links.note: Data-driven intelligence placed in the categorical Poll neighborhood, not only the Search; theory preserved because the CatMADS framework accepts any neighborhood; BO search step is the standard Method 1 move.
Outputs classified as relaxable-quantifiable, unrelaxable, hidden; ranking switches with incumbent feasibility; progressive barrier with feasible and infeasible incumbents.
Purpose-built mechanical-part blackbox plus the 60-problem Cat-Suite, public scripts and data; the illustrative problem is constructed, not a partner simulator.
Other-family competitors, common DoE, seeds, data profiles at three tau, S128 f0 rule; gaps: no BO competitor, no ablation.
CatMADS prototype built on NOMAD; GPs via SMT.
Categorical-variable pathology carried from framework to distance, benchmark suite, algorithm and neighborhoods in the Halle-Hannan line.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constraint pseudo-distance set to zero whenever both candidates are predicted feasible after an uncertainty relaxation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dominance ordering to merge two criteria
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Pareto-nondominated components first, zero-primary ties by secondary, rest by primary; primary switches with feasibility.
Surrogate-based neighborhoods do not affect convergence because the method remains an instance of CatMADS (shared with S155).

Show test-problem difficulty with per-category LHS feasibility rates at increasing sample sizes (pp. 7-8).

coauthors: E. Halle-Hannan (first and corresponding author), Y. Diouane, S. Le Digabel, C. Tribes

quotes.text: The work does not aim to introduce a new optimization method, but rather to provide additional structural information that facilitates handling categorical variables.
The surrogate-based neighborhoods introduced here do not affect the theoretical convergence results, as the proposed method remains an instance of the CatMADS framework.
